title: No artist, solo project this time. How far can AI actually take 3D assets for a commercial game?
author: Accomplished-Ball325
selftext:
I've made a few games with a small team before, but we never had a dedicated artist. This time I'm going fully solo, so the art is entirely on me, and I honestly have no idea where the realistic limit is for AI-generated 3D.

The GIF above is from a showcase game I built earlier. Every asset in it was bought from Unreal's Fab marketplace. If possible, that's roughly the quality level I'm hoping to reach with AI.

I tried hooking Claude up to Blender through MCP and asked it to build 3D assets. The results were a mess: broken topology, weird proportions, nothing I'd ship. I know my prompting was probably the problem, so I'm not blaming the tools.

For people who've actually shipped something, or gotten close:

* What does your pipeline look like for commercially usable 3D assets? Image-to-3D, text-to-3D, LLM + Blender scripting, or a mix?
* Which parts do you still do by hand (retopo, UVs, texturing, rigging)?
* How do you prompt or set up references so the output is consistent across a whole set of assets, not just one-offs?

Honestly, anything helps. Workflows, tools, mistakes you made, or even "don't bother, do X instead." I'd really appreciate any advice at all.

comments.author: zenmatrix83
comments.body: alot of its still needing an eye for what looks good, the video you shared has problems, the white sword animations look all kind of wrong. an ai can't catch these things, you need to know exactly what you want. The assets seem fine in the video, just animation , some lighting seems off. I do not light the 1 2 3 4 ui thing at the bottome left, its very hard to see. Again these types of thing no AI can fix without you tellint it.

replies.author: Accomplished-Ball325
replies.body: That's true. I don't know much about visual direction. I want to get better at it so I can write proper prompts for AI, but I don't even know what I should study to get there. I've asked AI the same question, but I couldn't get an answer that actually helped.

replies.author: zenmatrix83
replies.body: Look at each animation each shadow , does it make sense. There are shadows that bother me too, why are they there , should they be . Make she the light source casting them matches the actual light in the scene and don’t look just randomly added on. There are mistimed antimations where the swords don’t touch but they should, the movement looks forced, amount others . Go watch YouTube videos of similar games and go frame by frame watching the movement. Most of this is just repeatedly exposure to what looks good and what popular

comments.author: maxneuds
comments.body:
Hey Claude, take some assets and build Dark Souls at home for me.

What I currently do for 3D assets is multi view to 3D with local tools I am refining with Claude. Results are still in testing. Test to 3D haven't tested that yet. I prefer to fine tune concept images first for better art control.

comments.author: YeetCompleet
comments.body:
Tbh I think it's hard to get Claude to build 3D assets to a certain quality too. At some point you get to tweaking fine details on things and it starts to feel inefficient. I'm thinking a more collaborative approach is better where Claude hands off assets at like 90% of where you want it, and then you go into blender and add your tweaks on top. I've been thinking about this for clothing wrinkles, fixing up some collars, things like that. The downside is that I've been using the headless blender way where I've been building everything from a script that sits in the repository, and that just becomes obsolete. Once handed off, I can't go back to it, only MCP.

I think it's probably worth it though. I'm not artist but I've been having Claude teach me how to use blender to achieve what I want too.

comments.author: VictorBuildsApps
comments.body:
Making models with code took forever for me too. I start with a concept image and use a generator for things like characters and creatures.

A few days ago I ran a character, a creature, a barrel and a sword through a few generators, four tries per asset per generator. I'd start with Tripo P2 for the character and creature. Meshy T2.5 did the cleanest barrel at a 2,000 triangle target. The sword blades came out too thick, so I build those in Blender.

Even the usable meshes needed cleanup, things like welding, UV fixes and weights. I rig and animate in Blender. For characters with gear, I generate the body and gear separately and fit the pieces together there.

comments.author: DraconicBlade
comments.body:
The dumpster. This combat looks like ass, absolutely no feedback on animations for hits and successful block/parries.

The two models may as well not even be in the same game, they don't interact at all.

Go look at a perfect parry in any soulslop rated above a 4 /10 and tell me how far you think this is going. Maybe youll get a 2 if your protag has less clothing.

comments.author: Kindly-Sail6260
comments.body: You need Tripo or a dedicated 3d AI generator to get anything close to a high quality and then you need to decide whether or not you need to separate body parts and put them back together. Accessories will also be another generation. Tripo does a pretty decent job for what you want it to do. Just keep in mind that this will all take time for you to make anything of high quality or a finished product. So be ready to grind out the boring days of game development.
